title: Slowing Ships Down Saves Giant Whales — But Will the Rule Stay?
summary: Have you ever been so focused on a snack that you didn't notice someone right next to you? That's kind of what happens with North Atlantic right whales. These giant animals — they can weigh up to 80,000 pounds! — spend a lot of time near the surface eating, and they don't always pay attention to boats. Since 2008, a rule has made big ships slow down in certain areas along the U.S. East Coast to avoid hitting these whales. And it's worked: research shows slowing down can cut deadly collisions by up to 90 percent. But now, the government agency NOAA is wondering if the rule is still necessary. They're looking into whether high-tech whale-detection systems could replace speed limits. Conservationists are worried. Only about 380 North Atlantic right whales are left in the wild, making them one of the most endangered whale species on Earth. Every whale matters, especially females that can have many calves. For example, a whale named Wart has added at least 31 whales to the population! Ship strikes have killed at least 15 right whales since 2017, even with the speed rule. Experts say weakening protections could push the species closer to extinction. The good news? 2026 has seen the best calving season since 2009, giving a glimmer of hope. But as one scientist put it, "We're one more bad year away from a number they can't rebound from." So, will the speed limit stay? That's a question that could decide the fate of these gentle giants.
why_it_matters: The choices we make today about boats and whales could decide if you'll get to see a right whale in the wild when you grow up, or only in books.

background_read: Right whales got their name because whalers hundreds of years ago thought they were the 'right' ones to hunt — they swam slowly and floated when killed.
NOAA (the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, a U.S. agency that studies oceans and weather) created the ship speed rule in 2008 because too many whales were being hit.
Even with protection, ship strikes and fishing gear entanglements remain the biggest threats to this species, which is why conservationists fear any rollback of the rules.
Article_Structure: WHO: North Atlantic right whales, conservationists, and NOAA
WHAT: A 2008 rule that forces big ships to slow down to protect whales is being re-examined, even though it cuts deadly collisions by 90%
WHERE: Along the U.S. East Coast where the whales feed and migrate
WHY: Because the whale population is critically low (only about 380 left) and every death brings them closer to extinction, but NOAA is considering technology instead of speed limits

perspectives.description: They say removing the speed rule now, when only about 380 whales remain, is reckless. Even one bad year could collapse the population beyond recovery.

Some shipping companies and NOAA are interested in high-tech whale-detection systems that could alert captains to slow down only when whales are near, saving time and money while still protecting whales.
Biologists point out that the calmest mothers like Wart keep the species going, and young calves are most at risk from ship strikes, so steady protections are crucial until the population stabilizes.
